definition: Lingering means lasting longer than expected and slow to fade or leave.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word lingering. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know lingering should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A lingering frost kept the garden gray into May, and the tulips finally came up looking apologetic.
Residual is milder than lingering: a residual ache is the faint trace left after the injury is essentially over, while a lingering ache is still actively hanging on, taking its time to leave.
Persistent is stronger than lingering: a lingering cough is slow to fade on its own, while a persistent one digs in and refuses to leave no matter what the doctor throws at it.
Persistent means refusing to leave — it digs in and outlasts every effort to be rid of it. Lingering is gentler: the thing is going, just slowly, and nobody has to fight it.
Residual names what is left over once the rest is gone — a fixed trace, measured after the fact. Lingering describes the leaving itself: something still mid-fade, present past its expected end.

Lingering means lasting longer than expected and slow to fade or leave.
When the stitches came out, the surgeon warned Maya about a lingering stiffness in the wrist — nothing dangerous, just slow to leave.
She noticed it all summer; by October it visited only on cold mornings, a fainter guest each week.
The stiffness is neither permanent nor gone.

It stays past the point where she expected it to end and fades by degrees, and that unhurried overstaying is what lingering marks: the word looks at something on its way out and notices how slowly the exit happens.
Lingering watches an exit happen slowly, and it takes whatever tone its noun gives it — a lingering perfume is wistful, a lingering doubt is unwelcome.

Inside this unit, keep the lanes: belated is about arriving after the proper time, lingering about leaving after it; and where an evanescent thing is gone before you can name it, a lingering one is still here after it should have gone.

The forecast said the heat wave would break on Labor Day, and technically it did.
But a lingering warmth hung on for most of September — mornings that needed no jacket, lake water still soft enough for swimming a full three weeks after the lifeguards left.
Nobody minded, and nobody did anything about it — there was nothing to fight.
The pool stayed open an extra week, and the ice-cream cart did a quiet, steady business.
The hardware store kept its fans in the window until the first of October, then moved them out, unhurried, the way the season itself was leaving.
By the time the maples turned, the warmth was a memory.
It had not been driven out; it had simply taken its time saying goodbye.
